newsitem.title: UK: UK stocks face October jitters in coming week.
newsitem.headline: UK stocks face October jitters in coming week.

text.p: As UK shares continue to bump up against all-time highs, further records could be on the cards next week despite continuing signs that UK economic growth is running fast enough to renew concerns of an upturn in inflation.
Yet as the October 19 anniversary of the 1987 crash passes, markets may also be reminded that October is often a time for the markets to suffer unusual and unwelcome volatility.
Three companies in the UK's FTSE 100 index report results next week and the UK market will also have a spate of domestic economic data, including September retail sales to digest.

In the U.S. there are few major economic indicators, perhaps depriving world markets of fresh impetus, though the flow of third-quarter U.S. company results continues after a week of positive surprises which helped send the Dow to new records.
Some strategists believe the FTSE 100 is flying in the face of economic reality and could be brought down to earth with a bump on growing risks of a rise in interest rates.

At Charterhouse Tilney, strategist Richard Jeffrey is one who argues UK markets could be undercut by growing worries over the need for Chancellor Kenneth Clarke to raise rates to ward off inflation pressures.

"Having burst through the 4,000 level, the equity market has failed to make further substantial progress over the past two weeks," Jeffrey said. "Economic data are beginning to raise the spectre of inflation and pressure is building on Clarke to act."

Perhaps even worse, if Clarke leaves rates unchanged to encourage a "feel-good factor" ahead of the election which must be held by next May, then worries could escalate that even greater rate hikes are in prospect next year.
Robin Griffiths, chart analyst at HSBC James Capel -- who expects the FTSE 100 to peak above 4,400 early in 1997 -- said he expects shares to rally from any short-term loss.

"If we have a setback late October, and late October is when we get them, maybe because of something like a crisis in Russia which sends the FTSE down 100 points or so, you must go in and buy," Griffiths said.

"At this stage in the bull market you would expect volatility to increase," he said, "but once we are through October we are into the strongest three months of the year, which are Novemebr, December and January."
Griffiths dismissed fears that inflation risks could derail the advance.
"Bull markets always climb a wall of worry," he said, noting that institutions are holding a higher-than-average eight percent cash after recent strong dividend payouts.
"The need is to find things to buy rather than sell."

Events of the the past week are anyway a sign that UK markets may continue to make progress as long as U.S. stocks and bonds head upwards, despite the domestic economic background -- though the UK may underperform.
"We'd certainly sign up to idea that there is more of an inflation risk in the UK than elsewhere," said Ian Scott, equity strategist at Lehman Brothers.
"But beyond the confines of the UK, markets around the world have been strong of late," Scott added.

"The logic comes via the bond markets, if you have yields falling around the world, even if gilts don't participate fully, it would be surprising to see gilt yields rising. The linkage is very strong."

UK economic reports next include UK retail sales on Wednesday and third quarter GDP on Friday. UK companies reporting include Imperial Chemical Industries, Wolseley and SmithKline Beecham. In the U.S. the main economic release is durable goods orders on Friday. -- London Newsroom, +44 171 542 5106
